title: The Garbage Man: Bill Gates Has Earned Billions Investing in Climate-Polluting Landfills
author: Alex Cuadros
content:
In November 2015, world leaders descended on Paris to negotiate a historic
agreement to limit global warming. But on the summit's opening day, attention
turned to a private citizen slouched awkwardly in a chair on stage: Bill
Gates.

Gates, with his characteristic flop of sandy hair, grinned impishly as
President Barack Obama called him a “visionary” and a “driving force” behind a
pair of pledges that both saw as key to the larger agreement. First the
world's largest economies would double their spending on research into clean-
energy technologies. Then investors like Gates would back the startups that
emerged. The Microsoft cofounder had already enlisted two dozen other
billionaires to join the effort.

For Gates, who’d become increasingly consumed by this unprecedented threat to
human well-being, the moment marked his arrival as a leading figure in the
fight against climate change.

“If we back over 50 different breakthrough approaches, we know that several of
those will give us the solution that we need,” Gates said during his own
speech. He would invest at least $2 billion of his own money in companies
developing geothermal wells, new kinds of nuclear reactors and machines that
[pull carbon from the air](https://www.heirloomcarbon.com/), to name just a
few.

With much less fanfare, however, Gates has put more than double that amount
into a very dirty, old-school industry. At the time of the Paris summit, he
was already the dominant shareholder of America’s No. 2 landfill operator,
Republic Services. He has since increased his stake to 38% of the company, a
position worth $29 billion.

### Bill Gates’ Stake in Republic Services, a Landfill Operator, Now Exceeds a
Fifth of His Net Worth

![An area chart showing how much of Bill Gates’ net worth comes from two
companies and other sources. Microsoft started at nearly 100% in 2000 and fell
to about 24% in 2026. Republic Services started at near 0% in 2000 and rose to
about 22% in 2026. The rest is grouped under “Other,” which rose from 0% in
2000 to 53% in 2026.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2027/10/stock-share-mobile.png)Note: "Other" includes stakes
in other publicly traded companies and accumulated dividends and investment
returns. Sources: Forbes’ The World's Billionaires, Bloomberg’s Billionaires
Index, SEC filings, StockAnalysis.com Chris Alcantara/ProPublica

While fossil fuels get most of the attention, scientists increasingly see
landfills as a crucial climate issue. They're responsible for as much as a
fifth of the [country’s emissions of
methane](https://acp.copernicus.org/articles/24/5069/2024/), a highly potent
greenhouse gas, studies show. Republic alone generates as much climate
pollution as [3 million gasoline-burning
cars](https://republicservicesinc.gcs-web.com/static-files/2025-Republic-
Services-GRI-Report.pdf#page=22) each year, according to its own reports.

One might imagine that a landfill operator with Gates as its largest
shareholder — and with three people closely linked to Gates on its board —
would lead the way in tackling those emissions. Even after seemingly softening
his stance on global warming in a [controversial blog
post](https://www.gatesnotes.com/three-tough-truths-about-climate) last year,
Gates remains one of the world’s most prominent voices on the issue. As he did
in his bestselling 2021 book “How to Avoid a Climate Disaster,” he continues
to [advocate for cutting emissions](https://www.gatesnotes.com/home/home-page-
topic/reader/for-an-affordable-climate-win-look-to-the-sky), and he has called
on his fellow business leaders to do their part.

Gates, though, has failed to make Republic live up to his own climate
principles, a ProPublica investigation has found. Federal inspectors have
repeatedly found methane escaping from Republic landfills at levels above
federal limits. The company has refrained from adopting the ambitious
emissions-reduction goal embraced by its main competitor. Republic has even
lobbied against policies that could make the wider industry cleaner, including
by [keeping organic waste out of
landfills](https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2016-12/documents/landfill-
nsps-eg-2016-rtc.pdf#page=100) in the first place.

“It seems very likely that Bill Gates has the power to influence Republic's
behavior to make it more climate-friendly, even if that costs the company
profits,” said Ann Lipton, a legal scholar who studies corporate governance at
the University of Colorado, Boulder.

As for whether he should, in her words, “put his money where his mouth is,”
Lipton said, “you can leave it to the reader to make the moral judgment.”

### Gates' Climate Awakening

Gates didn't respond to repeated requests to discuss his landfill investments,
and ProPublica couldn't find any public comments he’s made about them. But the
bet has proven wildly lucrative. Since November 1999, when he emerged as the
owner of 5% of Republic's shares — “[It's ‘Garbage In’ for
Gates](https://nypost.com/1999/11/19/its-garbage-in-for-gates-invests-114m-in-
huizengas-republic/),” the New York Post headline read — the company's stock
price has soared thirtyfold. And Gates has personally received $2.6 billion in
dividends, a ProPublica analysis of securities filings shows.

In those early days, Gates hadn't yet awakened to the threat of global
warming. It was a different time. Microsoft Windows ran on more than 80% of
personal computers. Gates was the world’s richest person, and his bespectacled
face [graced the cover of
Time](https://content.time.com/time/covers/0,16641,19990322,00.html) magazine
[twice that
year](https://content.time.com/time/covers/0,16641,19991115,00.html). He was
simultaneously criticized for what a federal judge determined to be
[Microsoft’s monopolistic practices](https://www.justice.gov/atr/us-v-
microsoft-courts-findings-fact) and admired for establishing what was soon to
become the world's largest charitable foundation.

A rare clue to why Gates made his foray into landfills can be found in an
[interview he gave to
Fortune](https://web.archive.org/web/20141018211812/http://archive.fortune.com/magazines/fortune/fortune_archive/1999/03/15/256491/index.htm)
that year. To fund his plan to give away virtually his entire fortune, he said
he’d given his personal money manager, Michael Larson, a simple remit: Sell
Microsoft shares, buy safe, boring assets.

Republic’s then-chairman, [billionaire Wayne
Huizenga](https://www.propublica.org/article/clarence-thomas-other-
billionaires-sokol-huizenga-novelly-supreme-court), had flown Larson by
helicopter to his private golf course in Florida, according to the article.
It’s unclear if Huizenga pitched Republic there, but it fit the remit. America
would always produce trash, ensuring a steady stream of revenue. After that
initial investment, Larson progressively increased Gates' stake in Republic
over the years that followed. Larson would also acquire a small chunk of
Republic's main competitor, Waste Management — which Huizenga also once led —
on behalf of the Gates Foundation.

It was only in 2006, when he asked two climate scientists to educate him, that
Gates started to grasp the potentially [“catastrophic” effects of greenhouse
gases](https://books.google.com/books/about/How_to_Avoid_a_Climate_Disaster.html?id=qmuTEAAAQBAJ),
he later wrote. But he also saw that the poorest people in the world needed
more energy to improve their lot. The solution, he concluded, was something
climate activists often underplay: innovation that could [make clean energy
cheap enough](https://www.ted.com/talks/bill_gates_innovating_to_zero) to
naturally displace fossil fuels. That was the idea behind Breakthrough Energy,
the initiative he launched in Paris in 2015.

![Three seated men in suits are clapping their hands. The man furthest to the
right looks directly at the camera while the others look in the opposite
direction.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2027/10/GettyImages-499274812.jpg?w=2560)Microsoft co-founder
Bill Gates, right, then-U.S. President Barack Obama, left, and then-French
President François Hollande applaud a speech during the United Nations
conference on climate change in Paris in 2015. Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images

Around the same time, methane began to emerge as a focus of climate action.
The gas can trap 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide in the near term, and
it's responsible for [one-third of the global
warming](https://www.unep.org/en/publications/report/eye-methane-2024) we
experience today, according to the United Nations Environment Programme. But
it also breaks down much more quickly, turning into CO2 and water vapor in
about a decade — which means that cutting methane emissions now would reduce
that warming within our lifetimes. This is especially urgent, scientists say,
as the [climate approaches tipping
points](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/01/04/magazine/amazon-tipping-point.html)
that could doom rainforests, coral reefs and ice sheets.

In speeches and interviews, Gates has sometimes warned about methane, but
usually from agricultural sources (“[cow farts](https://www.gatesnotes.com/we-
should-discuss-soil-as-much-as-coal),” in his words). He has rarely mentioned
landfills, even after Larson — who still runs Gates’ investment office,
Cascade Asset Management — joined Republic's board in 2009. Gates' stake in
the company, though, was a relatively small portion of his own net worth until
fairly recently. And as Larson put it to Fortune, “I’ll call Bill about
something I'm buying if he needs to know, but Bill might not have any idea
what Cascade owns.” (Gates' Republic holdings are publicly disclosed in
securities filings.)

Elsewhere in Gatesworld, people started to home in on the climate threat posed
by landfills. The root of the issue is that landfills store buried trash — and
when organic waste decomposes underground, in the absence of oxygen, it
generates methane. The Gates Foundation has [funded research and
advocacy](https://www.globalmethanehub.org/waste/) aimed at solving that
problem, and Breakthrough has backed at least two early-stage companies
developing their own solutions. One, Windfall Bio, uses microbes to digest
methane into fertilizer. [Its product was actually
tested](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-
release/2025/07/10/3113185/0/en/sunshine-canyon-landfill-deploys-windfall-bio-
s-biocover-technology-in-field-trial.html) last year at a Republic landfill in
California, where the [pink liquid](https://www.washingtonpost.com/climate-
solutions/interactive/2025/methane-emissions-microbes/) was sprinkled on the
soil covering the top layer of trash.

Windfall said the test worked, substantially reducing emissions, but [the
startup reportedly ceased operations](https://agfundernews.com/exclusive-
waste-methane-to-fertilizer-startup-windfall-bio-auctions-off-assets) after a
[Department of Energy grant was
canceled](https://www.latitudemedia.com/news/scoop-these-are-the-321-awards-
doe-is-canceling/). (Windfall didn't respond to emailed requests for comment.)

On the surface, Republic has pursued a path consistent with Gates’ mission. In
2019, it became the first U.S. landfill operator to sign up for the Science
Based Targets Initiative, [promising to cut its
emissions](https://media.republicservices.com/2019-09-23-Republic-Services-
First-U-S-Recycling-and-Solid-Waste-Services-Provider-to-Set-SBTi-Approved-
Science-Based-Target-to-Reduce-Greenhouse-Gas-Emissions) by 35% by 2030. Not
that this was charity. Republic’s “climate leadership” became part of its
[pitch for garbage-collection contracts](https://www.recyclesmart.org/wp-
content/uploads/2024/10/Republic-Food-scraps.pdf#page=150) in progressive
cities and counties. The company also won placements on stock indexes for
businesses that meet certain [environmental, social and governance
criteria](https://media.republicservices.com/2025-01-10-Republic-Services-
Again-Named-to-Dow-Jones-Sustainability-World-and-North-America-Indices),
attracting sustainability-minded investors.

Still, a fundamental tension remained — one at the heart of Gates' vision. As
Republic’s then-CEO Donald Slager put it on a 2017 call with investors, “You
can’t have sustainability without profitability.”

### A Not-So-Model Landfill

Each day, Americans throw away melon rinds, salmon skins and half-eaten
drumsticks, paper towels, cheese that was too funky and eggs a day past their
sell-by date. They discard greasy pizza boxes with crusts still rattling
around inside and unthinkable amounts of leftover Chinese takeout. Not to
mention the occasional dead pet.

![Clouds of dust hang over the mound at a large-scale municipal landfill on a
sunny day.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2027/10/20260929-Felix-Gates-Landfills-017.jpg)Dust is kicked
up by trucks and bulldozers at Republic Service’s McCarty Road Landfill in
Houston. Mark Felix for ProPublica

Most of that trash — 240 million tons a year, enough to bury Manhattan under
100 feet of refuse — is hauled to one of the country's 1,400 active landfills,
where hulking vehicles with spiked wheels crush it into thin layers. At the
end of each day, bulldozers typically spread soil on top, and for almost
everyone who produced that trash, it will forever remain out of sight and out
of mind.

[People who live near landfills](https://lapublicpress.org/2025/03/sunshine-
canyon-landfill-smell-complaints-violations/), though, describe smelling
rotten cabbage, rotten eggs and rotten fish, as well as ammonia and skunk. Or
as a neighbor to one Republic landfill put it: “I started smelling this stench
like burning diapers. … It was foul.” Some describe burning throats, burning
eyes, [headaches and nausea](https://www.hcn.org/issues/57-6/where-the-
garbage-goes/).**** And while methane itself has no scent, those odors
indicate that [the gas is being
released](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/ab7b99),
studies show.  

Still, modern landfills are an undeniable improvement over what came before.
[Open dumping and burning](https://www.wastedive.com/news/resource-
conservation-recovery-act-1976-epa-landfill/833389/) remained widespread until
the 1970s. It was only in the ’90s that federal regulators started requiring
operators to collect leachate (garbage juice, which can contaminate
groundwater) and, at larger facilities, landfill gas (which is typically about
half methane and half carbon dioxide but can also contain carcinogens like
benzene).

Industry experts often compare landfills to living, breathing creatures.
Underground trash inevitably shifts and settles, making it difficult to [keep
that gas from escaping](https://rmi.org/resources/waste-methane-101-driving-
emissions-reductions-from-landfills/). Managing such a beast is costly, which
helps to explain why smaller operations have increasingly given way to
corporations like Republic, which can turn a profit through economies of
scale.

Republic declined to make executives available for interviews or to allow
ProPublica to visit a landfill. But in May 2022 — around the same time Gates
was lobbying for the passage of President Joe Biden’s [historic climate
bill](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2022-08-16/how-bill-gates-
lobbied-to-save-the-climate-tax-bill-biden-just-signed) — the company invited
the Houston Chronicle to its local McCarty Road Landfill. Opened a half
century earlier, the facility had passed through two corporate owners before
being swallowed up by Republic, and now it was the site of a very Gatesian
kind of project.

On the day of the visit, gulls circled hungrily as workers in neon vests gave
a [tour of the gas-collection
system](https://www.houstonchronicle.com/business/energy/article/Gas-happens-
Houston-company-launches-ambitious-17219996.php). Like at most other large
landfills in the country, wells had been drilled deep into the trash below —
five hundred of them in total. The top of each well sprouted from the grassy
slopes in the form of a stubby black pipe fitted with a valve for adjusting
the flow of underground gas. The workers also showed off large, bright blue,
snail-shaped “blowers” — machines that suck that gas into a network of
pipelines, then push it to the clanking, humming on-site plant that turns it
into a salable product.

![A man in a fluorescent yellow vest and safety hat stands near pipes coming
out of the ground at a landfill while billowy white clouds fill a blue sky
above.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2027/10/GettyImages-2191080435.jpg?w=2560)A Republic worker
stands next to a gas well at the company's McCarty Road Landfill in Houston in
2022. Houston Chronicle/Hearst Newspapers

Most landfills that are required to collect gas [simply burn it
off](https://www.epa.gov/lmop/frequent-questions-about-landfill-
gas?utm_source=chatgpt.com#doeseparegulate). But they can also process it into
“renewable natural gas,” which is functionally equivalent to the version
pumped by oil companies. In part because this reuses the carbon from
decomposing waste, it's generally [considered more climate-
friendly](https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2020-07/documents/lmop_rng_document.pdf).
It also turns an environmental liability into a source of revenue — exactly
the kind of win-win that Gates has long championed.

Yet the technology is no guarantee that the climate is being protected. In
fact, it may be just the opposite.

In September 2024, the Environmental Protection Agency issued an “enforcement
alert” saying that landfills across the country were “[violating monitoring
and maintenance requirements](https://www.epa.gov/enforcement/enforcement-
alert-epa-finds-msw-landfills-are-violating-monitoring-and-maintenance).”
While the EPA didn’t name the operators, ProPublica obtained the corresponding
spreadsheet through a public records request, and a fifth of the facilities
targeted belong to Republic.

McCarty, far from being a model landfill, was among the worst offenders. It
would soon earn Republic a formal “[finding of
violation](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28858083-mccarty-landfill-
epa-finding-of-violation/)” for allegedly failing to detect “exceedances” —
methane escaping at levels above federal limits — for years on end. The EPA
also noted repeated failures to address flooded wells, gullies formed by
erosion and trash peeking through the surface of the landfill. Despite
Republic’s economic incentive to capture methane, EPA inspectors found
evidence of “poor maintenance” and “careless operation” of the gas-collection
system as well.

And McCarty is hardly an outlier. Recent studies suggest that landfills with
renewable natural gas facilities [can actually emit more
methane](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/full/10.1021/acs.est.4c07572?ref=vi_climate-
action) than those that only burn off the gas or use it to generate
electricity. One possible explanation is that methane concentrations can vary
across different parts of a landfill. According to researchers at Carbon
Mapper, a NASA partner that measures emissions from various industries, some
operators may prioritize collecting [gas with higher methane
content](https://rmi.org/app/uploads/dlm_uploads/2025/07/2025-07-US-landfill-
methane-fact-sheet.pdf#page=3), which is cheaper to process — allowing more of
the remaining methane to leak out.

Republic spokesperson Rob Litt declined to comment on whether that happened at
McCarty, but said in a statement, “We employ hundreds of environmental
managers and engineers. … If issues are identified, we work to resolve them.”

“Protecting the environment is part of Republic Services’ business,” he added.

The issues aren't exclusive to landfills with natural gas facilities. Since
2020, EPA inspectors have used handheld methane detectors to sweep at least 39
of Republic’s roughly 200 landfills, according to inspection reports obtained
by ProPublica. Including the issues at McCarty, they documented more than
1,400 problem spots — ranging from animal burrows to choked-off wells —
spewing excessive amounts of methane.

In some cases, methane could be seen bubbling up through dark, fetid leachate
pools. In others, so much methane was being released — with concentrations
between 100 and 300 times the federal limit — that it was an explosion hazard.

### Methane Bubbles at a Republic Services Landfill

Methane bubbles up through a pool of liquid drained from the trash at
Republic's Apex Regional Landfill in Nevada, documented by EPA inspectors in
2024. Environmental Protection Agency

### What the Satellites Saw

Around the time of the Houston Chronicle visit, Republic’s CEO, a former
McKinsey consultant named Jon Vander Ark, was promoting a new slogan:
“Sustainability in action.” Meanwhile, though, Republic was quietly shying
away from true climate leadership.

In 2021, two years after Republic signed on to the Science Based Targets
Initiative, the SBTI made its [minimum climate
goal](https://sciencebasedtargets.org/news/sbti-raises-the-bar-to-1-5-c) much
more ambitious. Waste Management (where the Gates Foundation owns a small
minority of the shares) would soon adopt it.

This was just months after Gates published “How to Avoid a Climate Disaster,”
in which he exhorted private companies “to embrace the harder steps” toward
solving global warming. Republic staff calculated that the new SBTI target
could require more than $1 billion in additional spending on gas wells and
other improvements, according to a former employee. Though that is less than
half of what Republic has spent on dividends for Gates alone, it would leave
less money for the company to redistribute to him and other shareholders.
Republic has also spent more than $8 billion [buying its own
stock](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/LSB10266) in the open market,
ProPublica's analysis shows, likely boosting the value of shares held by
investors.

The matter was finally presented to the board around the second half of 2024,
this person said. By then the board included Larson, Gates’ longtime
investment manager — whose “[insight into sustainability
issues](https://republicservicesinc.gcs-web.com/node/27601/html)” is cited in
company filings — and three other people with business ties to Gates (one has
since left). While that is only four board members among a total of 13, Gates’
dominant shareholding means that, “as a practical matter, on any matter that
gets voted on, he will almost certainly control the outcome,” said Lipton, the
corporate-governance expert.

Republic never made the leap, and now it walks an awkward line. It continues
to tout its affiliation with the SBTI while saying, in a note buried deep in
one of its many sustainability reports, that the more ambitious target is
“[not an immediate strategic
priority](https://investor.republicservices.com/static-
files/3dfdd1f3-f4cd-405f-a6ba-17d567bcdecd#page=56).”

Per SBTI rules, Republic has until the end of this year to [submit an updated
target](https://sciencebasedtargets.org/faqs#25804). But when ProPublica asked
if it would, the spokesperson said only, “We are reviewing our goals.” He
declined to comment on the estimated cost or the board discussions.

![A Republic sign and a rusted yellow tractor sitting inside a circle of
landscaping bricks. ](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2027/10/20260929-Felix-Gates-Landfills-003-1.jpg?w=2560)The
entrance to Republic's McCarty Road Landfill in Houston Mark Felix for
ProPublica ![Several large trucks, including a tractor-trailer and a trash
collection truck, enter and exit a driveway leading to a landfill. In a
driver-side car mirror, a line of trucks is waiting to
enter.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2027/10/20260929-Felix-
Gates-Landfills-002.jpg?w=2560)Garbage trucks pull in and out of the McCarty
landfill. Mark Felix for ProPublica

There is, though, an even larger issue with Republic’s climate claims.

In line with its existing SBTI goal, Republic says it has already [cut its
landfill emissions](https://republicservicesinc.gcs-web.com/static-
files/2025-Republic-Services-GRI-Report.pdf#page=22) by 20% since 2017. But
that figure isn’t based on actual measurements of methane escaping from its
facilities. According to the method cited in its sustainability reports,
Republic instead typically measures the methane collected by its wells. Then
it extrapolates how much it’s failing to collect — and how much is being
emitted — based on the characteristics of each facility.

This method is based on an industry study that, [as the EPA has
noted](https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2024-04/ghgrp-final-
preamble-and-rule-april-2024.pdf#page=215), excluded data from gas-collection
systems that were “[not working well](https://www.scsengineers.com/wp-
content/uploads/2015/03/Sullivan_SWICS_White_Paper_Version_2.2_Final.pdf#page=19).”
The EPA's own reporting rules allow the same basic approach, which can cause
companies collecting less gas due to a “malfunction or inefficiency” to
“[erroneously report decreasing
emissions](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/388078194_Satellite_monitoring_of_annual_US_landfill_methane_emissions_and_trends),”
according to a 2025 study using satellite data by researchers at Harvard, NASA
and Carbon Mapper. The researchers specifically examined two Republic
landfills, and at one of them, the company reported declining emissions to the
EPA even though satellite measurements showed they had risen over a four-year
period.

The reporting gaps can be enormous. A study led by Hannah Nesser, now at
Georgetown, found Republic facilities to be the [No. 1 and No. 2
emitters](https://acp.copernicus.org/articles/24/5069/2024/) among the roughly
70 large U.S. landfills the researchers observed over the course of 2019. The
first, the National Serv-All Landfill in Indiana, was found to be releasing an
astounding 13 times as much methane as what the company reported to the EPA.
And that pattern repeated to varying degrees across three-quarters of the
Republic landfills in the study. (McCarty wasn't in the study, but according
to [measurements by Carbon
Mapper](https://data.carbonmapper.org/?plume_id=tan20260918t182331c51s4001-A&details=CH4_6A_1000m_-95.23800_29.82683%3Fstatus%3Dnot_deleted#13.97/29.82636/-95.23188),
it emits more than twice what the company has reported.)

In response to questions about these studies, the Republic spokesperson said,
“We stand by the sustainability results we’ve achieved.”

He also pointed to a letter from the National Waste and Recycling Association,
a major trade group, [questioning the
accuracy](https://www.aqmd.gov/docs/default-source/agendas/hearing-board/case-
documents/chiquita--6177/exhibit-dddd---nwra-and-swana-america-comments-on-
non-regulatory-public-docket-municipal-solid-waste-
landfills.pdf?sfvrsn=faff9c61_2#page=140) of satellite measurements. It is a
tactic from the playbook of another major climate polluter, the oil and gas
industry, said Katherine Blauvelt of Full Circle Future, which advocates for
cleaning up landfills.

“Satellites, peer-reviewed research studies and EPA inspectors on the ground
all keep finding the same thing: unchecked and underreported methane
emissions,” she said. “There's a fire alarm going off and instead of getting
out the extinguisher, the waste industry is blaming the smoke detector."

### Quietly Fighting Climate Policies

Last year, Gates published a blog post criticizing the [“doomsday view” of
global warming](https://www.gatesnotes.com/three-tough-truths-about-climate) —
a striking shift for someone who'd once warned of the failing ecosystems,
[mass migration and soaring mortality](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/bill-
gates-climate-change-disaster-60-minutes-2021-02-14/) that could result from
hotter temperatures. That led climate skeptics, including President Donald
Trump, to [say that Gates had
admitted](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/115459641125796285)
he was wrong. But Gates called that a “gigantic misreading.” While he believed
more lives could be saved by improving global health, where he’d decided to
shift his resources, he remained a “[climate
activist](https://www.latimes.com/environment/story/2025-11-05/gates-backs-up-
climate-memo-caltech),” he told one audience.

Gates has tried to lead by example. In 2019, he sold his shares in oil and gas
companies because, he later wrote, “[I don’t want to
profit](https://books.google.com/books/about/How_to_Avoid_a_Climate_Disaster.html?id=qmuTEAAAQBAJ)
if their stock prices go up because we don’t develop zero-carbon
alternatives.” He kept flying by private jet, but he “offset” those emissions
by buying credits from a company that removes carbon from the air. He has also
called on other business leaders to “make sure that [they’re not holding
back](https://hbr.org/podcast/2021/02/bill-gates-on-how-business-leaders-can-
fight-climate-change)” climate policies, even if those policies could cut into
profits.

![A man poses with a shiny new shovel on a sunny day while several individuals
take pictures of him. A yellow-and-black excavator vehicle is in the
background.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2027/10/h_16457930.jpg?w=2560)Bill Gates attends the
groundbreaking for TerraPower's nuclear power plant near Kemmerer, Wyoming, in
2024. Benjamin Rasmussen/The New York Times/Redux

Republic has actively worked against such policies — and yet Gates, according
to securities filings, has never sold a share.

In the final year of the Biden administration, the EPA announced a plan to
update its landfill gas rules, which have changed little since the ’90s. Among
other potential changes, [the agency asked for
comments](https://www.epa.gov/stationary-sources-air-pollution/non-regulatory-
public-docket-municipal-solid-waste-landfills) on the newer technologies, such
as satellites and drones, that research has found to be effective in
[monitoring and controlling methane
pollution](https://rmi.org/app/uploads/dlm_uploads/2024/03/wasteMAP_united_states_playbook.pdf).

Some landfill operators were already experimenting with these innovations. But
they wanted [almost all of it to remain
voluntary](https://swana.org/docs/default-source/advocacy-documents/nwra-and-
swana-white-paper-response-5-23-25-combined-final.pdf?sfvrsn=afaeca5b_2),
according to a joint statement from the National Waste and Recycling
Association and the Solid Waste Association of North America, both of which
have Republic executives on their boards.

“We do not believe that any of these technologies are sufficiently developed,”
the industry groups said, adding that the various innovations were “not cost-
effective,” “reliable” or “transparent.”

The Republic spokesperson declined to comment on whether that lobbying goes
against its climate commitments.

“A lot of the issue comes down to the profit of the corporate landfill
operators and their resistance to do things that will eat into that,” said
Darin Schroeder of the Clean Air Task Force, a climate advocacy group.

Gates' press representatives didn't respond to questions about whether he's
aware of the issues at Republic — or whether he has independently investigated
the source of [a fifth of his
fortune](https://www.bloomberg.com/billionaires/profiles/william-h-gates/).
But ProPublica interviewed multiple former employees at Breakthrough Energy,
Gates’ clean-tech investment arm, who all spoke on condition of anonymity.
They each said they hadn’t even heard about his landfill holdings.

“I agree there’s a bit of a conundrum there,” said one high-ranking staffer
who was laid off last year. But this person added, “Based on my time with him,
I think he's very serious about climate change. This isn’t a vanity thing for
him.”

“My theory is that he probably doesn't have much involvement in those
investments,” said another laid-off staffer.

Gates' investment managers, at least, can't claim total ignorance. Larson and
Thomas Handley, a Cascade senior adviser, both participate actively in
Republic's board discussions, according to a fellow director who spoke on the
condition of anonymity to share details of those private discussions. The
board also receives regular management briefings, including “high level”
reports on the company’s lobbying and litigation over “[practices we could do
better](https://violationtracker.goodjobsfirst.org/?parent=republic-
services),” this director said. (Larson didn't return phone messages left by
ProPublica at his office, and Cascade didn't respond to a question about his
and Handley's involvement in Republic.)

It’s unclear if Gates himself ever learned of those reports. But he appears to
have an even larger blind spot on the issue. The waste industry doesn’t fit
neatly into his view of climate change as a problem to be solved mainly
through technological breakthroughs. Innovations can help, but the root of the
problem is the inescapable fact that, when organic waste decomposes in the
absence of oxygen, methane is produced.

Properly managing the waste we've already buried is only the first step, said
Riley Duren, the former NASA engineer who founded Carbon Mapper. "In
parallel,” he said, “reduce food waste. Full stop. Then divert organic waste
away from landfills to prevent future emissions.”

This isn’t a utopian fantasy. Germany started [phasing out the
landfilling](https://www.catf.us/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/waste-methane-
toolbox.pdf) of biodegradable waste in 1993, and its landfill methane
emissions have plunged by more than 90%. (That compares to a decline of 40% in
the U.S. over roughly the same period.) Within the U.S., California now
requires food scraps and yard trimmings to be collected for composting or
other uses, and state regulators found that the economic, climate and health
benefits [would ultimately outweigh the
costs](https://calrecycle.ca.gov/organics/slcp/).

In its glossy sustainability reports, Republic says that “organics recycling
plays an important role in our operations.” And in California, with its
mandatory collection rules, the company processed close to a million tons of
organic waste last year, much of that at composting facilities.

![An aerial photograph shows around two dozen garbage snaking along dirt roads
on the large bare mound of a landfill.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2027/10/20261029-Felix-Gates-Landfills-009.jpg?w=2560)A steady
stream of garbage trucks flows through Republic's McCarty Road Landfill in
Houston on a recent weekday.  Mark Felix for ProPublica. Aerial support by
LightHawk.

But that remains a small fraction of its business. Speaking to a different
kind of audience — investors — Republic has described landfilling, along with
dumpster collection, [as its most profitable
segments](https://www.roic.ai/quote/RSG/transcripts/2020-year/1-quarter). So
when the EPA floated a federal organics-diversion policy in 2024, the company,
along with the rest of the landfill industry, opposed this, too. Their
response invoked an argument often used by opponents to regulation: It should
be left to the states to decide.

“It's like you've got a mousetrap, and it catches mice,” said Robert Bullard,
a Texas Southern University professor widely seen as the father of the
environmental justice movement. “You've got a landfill, and it makes money —
big money. So why tinker with it?”
